sections.heading: Glamsterdam Gas Repricing Security Concerns
sections.summary: ChainSecurity presented exploitable patterns in deployed contracts caused by EIP-8037/8038 gas changes; 13 DeFi projects identified so far, analysis incomplete.
sections.body:
- ChainSecurity (Hubert) presented findings on how Glamsterdam repricing EIPs ([EIP-8037](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-8037) and [EIP-8038](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-8038)) can enable previously-invalid "evil transactions" to succeed against deployed contracts.
  - The focus is on transactions that did not work pre-Glamsterdam but do work post-Glamsterdam, not on honest transactions that stop working.
- A contrived example demonstrated how the self-destruct force-send trick, combined with the state gas reservoir refund mechanism, can cause a contract to update a user's balance (setting it to zero) without actually transferring ETH.
  - Under Glamsterdam, self-destruct can cost ~200,000 gas due to new-account state gas (~180,000). If it runs out of gas, the state gas is refunded immediately to the calling frame, giving the victim contract enough gas to execute the subsequent SSTORE.
  - Pre-Glamsterdam, 1/64 retained gas was insufficient to continue; post-Glamsterdam, the refund makes continuation possible.
- Broader categories of broken developer assumptions identified:
  - Hard-coded gas amounts (reserves or pass-through amounts)
  - Assumption that `gasleft()` only decreases within a single frame (no longer true)
  - Assumption that certain simple contracts (like self-destruct wrappers) cannot fail
  - Increased 1/64 retained gas making previously-insufficient gas sufficient to continue execution
  - Existing out-of-gas detection patterns in contracts can now be bypassed
- ChainSecurity searched via Sourcify regex and sampled mainnet transactions; found 13 DeFi projects affected and initiated responsible disclosure.
  - Search was explicitly not exhaustive; minor-impact findings (e.g., signature nonce invalidation) not yet reported.
  - Off-chain tools and front-ends not analyzed at all.
  - Reaching affected projects has been difficult due to AI spam in bug bounty submission channels.
- [ChainSecurity blog post](https://www.chainsecurity.com/blog/glamsterdam-gas/index.html) published with technical details.
- lightclient noted that many of these issues require malicious transaction crafting and would not be discovered simply by running on Sepolia; the patterns are far more subtle than hard-coding CALL gas costs.
- lightclient: "imo unless you hardcode the CALL gas, i feel like we shouldn't be breaking production contracts."

sections.heading: Impact Analysis and Mainnet Timeline
sections.summary: No mainnet date will be set until a thorough analysis of affected contracts is complete; analysis expected to take at least 2-3 weeks.
sections.body:
- Agreement: no decision on mainnet date until there is a clear, thorough understanding of the impacts on deployed contracts.
  - lightclient: "i dont think we should schedule mainnet until we have an answer here."
  - Potuz: "Security trumps timeliness of the fork 100%."
- Three tiers of possible response outlined by Ansgar:
  1. Mitigations completed in time for on-schedule December mainnet rollout.
  2. Delayed mainnet rollout with same Glamsterdam specs (more time for analysis and project upgrades).
  3. Changes to Glamsterdam specs themselves.
- Hubert estimated at least 2-3 weeks for a more comprehensive analysis of high-value contracts; scope depends on whether L2-deployed contracts and smaller projects are included.
- Maria Silva framed the decisive question as whether a large enough non-upgradable contract is affected, which would warrant spec changes; after Hubert's answer she concluded it is still unclear whether such contracts exist, so spec changes may still be needed.
- Fredrik confirmed a working group has been created, and outreach to analysis firms (including Dedaub) is underway; expects more information by ACDT next week.
- lightclient observed that Dedaub has historically done strong work codifying invariants and searching through all existing contracts.
- Toni Wahrstätter cautioned that restoring broken invariants (e.g., `gasleft()` never goes up) may not be trivial and could undo the core benefits of the repricing EIPs.
- lightclient argued that if sufficient funds or users rely on functionality that would break, the protocol should not break user space; the question of forcing protocol upgrades on app developers is extremely messy.
- Delaying Hoodi likely means a December mainnet fork is unrealistic, pushing mainnet into 2027.

sections.heading: Hoodi Fork Cancellation
sections.summary: Decision: Hoodi Glamsterdam fork (Oct 26) is canceled indefinitely; clients asked to cut new releases unscheduling it.
sections.body:
- Decision: the Glamsterdam fork on Hoodi, scheduled for October 26, is canceled with no new date set.
  - Rationale: preserve Hoodi on Fusaka specs so it remains a viable testnet if Glamsterdam specs change, and to maintain one testnet on each side of the fork for comparison.
- Key arguments for cancellation:
  - Daniel Lehrner and Potuz: if specs change, both Sepolia (already forked) and Hoodi (if forked) would be on incompatible specs, leaving no usable testnet for the new specs.
  - Potuz: redeploying Hoodi's decentralized validator set would be a significant pain.
  - lightclient: should worry about breaking contracts, not timelines.
- Parithosh confirmed pandaops + all client teams control ~73% of Hoodi stake, making a coordinated rollback feasible.
- Barnabas opened [hoodi PR #33](https://github.com/eth-clients/hoodi/pull/33) to unschedule the fork during the call.
- Logistics for rollback:
  - Barnabas recommended all clients cut new releases unscheduling Hoodi, rather than just advising rollback to prior versions.
  - Dustin (Nimbus): Nimbus vendors the Hoodi config directly from eth-clients/hoodi repo, so the repo PR is a prerequisite for their release.
  - Potuz (Prysm): some complexity with security patches bundled in the Hoodi-ready release, but still prefers delaying Hoodi.
  - Blog post to go out immediately recommending rollback or waiting for new client releases; to be updated as releases become available.
- Dima Gusakov (Lido): confirmed Lido can handle the delay; Lido has ~2.3 million stake on Hoodi across 30+ operators; will reach out to operators to roll back but cannot guarantee 100% compliance.
- Sepolia remains on post-Glamsterdam specs; Łukasz suggested a Glamsterdam V1/V2 approach if spec changes occur, but Potuz strongly opposed maintaining two fork versions long-term.
- Hoodi shadow fork was already launching during the call ([glamsterdam-hsf-0](https://dora.glamsterdam-hsf-0.ethpandaops.io)); Gloas activation ~45 minutes away at time of discussion.

sections.heading: ACDT Call Duration Extension
sections.summary: No objections to extending ACDT calls from 60 to 90 minutes; change approved.
sections.body:
- Barnabas proposed officially extending All Core Devs Testing (ACDT) calls from 60 minutes to 90 minutes, citing frequent overruns.
- No objections raised.
- Decision: ACDT calls will be 90 minutes going forward.

sections.heading: Dynamic Base Fee Calculation for Shorter Slots
sections.summary: Barnabas raised awareness of an EIP PR replacing hard-coded base fee fractions with derived calculations for variable slot times; most clients have reviewed.
sections.body:
- Barnabas presented [EIP PR #12552](https://github.com/ethereum/EIPs/pull/12552) which uses derived base fee calculations instead of hard-coded fractions, enabling testing of different seconds-per-slot values without EL code changes each time.
- Most clients have already reviewed and approved; Barnabas plans to work on merging it into the EIP.
- Awareness item: clients that haven't reviewed yet were asked to do so.

sections.heading: Hegota CFI Priority Ordering
sections.summary: A proposed priority-ordered list of CFI'd EIPs was shared for testing and devnet sequencing; accepted as a living document.
sections.body:
- A [proposed priority list](https://gist.github.com/nixorokish/1f17a8527d18fcc8d10370c9c1b5583e) compiled by Nixo was presented for rough ordering of CFI'd EIPs for testing and devnet inclusion.
- The list is intended as a living document, not strictly binding; can be reshuffled as EIP complexity or readiness changes.
- No objections to adopting this as the working V1.
- Spencer suggested that in future scoping processes, this ordered list should be created natively as EIPs are CFI'd.

sections.heading: CFI vs SFI Semantics and Scoping Process
sections.summary: Debate on whether CFI should imply default inclusion; broad agreement that CFI is a big decision and the bar for PFI-to-CFI should be higher.
sections.body:
- lightclient raised concern that some treat CFI as "default ship" while others treat it as "default do not ship," creating ambiguity that allows EIPs to slip through without a real "should Ethereum do this?" discussion.
  - Proposed that if CFI means default ship, the PFI-to-CFI bar must be much higher.
  - Argued every protocol change is risk (as demonstrated by 8037/8038); Ethereum should do the minimal changes necessary.
- Barnabas: "CFI -> default ship it, PFI -> default DFI it."
- Potuz disagreed strongly: CFI was explicitly created so that not all clients are forced to implement; it's for testing without commitment.
- Justin Florentine: CFI-to-SFI is where labor assessment happens; removing that step would be harmful.
- Mario Vega: warned of sunk cost fallacy — once time is invested in CFI implementation, it becomes politically difficult to reject.
- [EIP-7723](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-7723) states CFI signals intent to include in devnets and is similar to "concept ACK," not sufficient for mainnet deployment.
- Toni Wahrstätter: "There should just never be a 'weak' CFI" — keep weak proposals at PFI longer instead of using CFI to explore.
- Multiple participants agreed the CFI bar should be higher going forward; for Hegota, the focus should be on carefully evaluating CFI'd EIPs before SFI.
- Hegota currently has ~19 CFI'd EIPs on the EL side; not all expected to ship.

sections.heading: Next Devnet: Bogota Devnet 2 Scope
sections.summary: Decision: launch Bogota devnet 2 (EL-only) pre-Devcon with four new EIPs; first merged EL+CL devnet to follow after Devcon.
sections.body:
- Two options discussed: another EL-only devnet (bogota-devnet-2) or immediately merging EL and CL into hegota-devnet-0.
- Jihoon noted that FOCIL-frames interaction design is not mature enough for a combined devnet next week; FOCIL alone would be doable.
- Mario Vega: combining is valuable because FOCIL and frames have real interaction, but if Bogota is ready, shipping it has standalone testing value.
- lightclient: Geth could stretch to ship combined, but more confident in EL-only; concerned that Devcon travel will cause slippage if nothing ships this week.
- Decision: ship bogota-devnet-2 (EL-only) pre-Devcon; discuss interactions at Devcon in person; first post-Devcon devnet will be merged EL+CL.
- Four EIPs scoped for bogota-devnet-2:
  - [EIP-8253](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-8253): Bump nonce of zero-nonce storage accounts
  - [EIP-4758](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-4758): Deactivate SELFDESTRUCT
  - [EIP-8298](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-8298): SETCODEFROM Code Reuse Instruction
  - [EIP-8151](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-8151): Account Code Restricted ecRecover
- Also includes the frames max_fee spec change from [EIP PR #12414](https://github.com/ethereum/EIPs/pull/12414), which lightclient planned to merge after the call.
- Client readiness: Nethermind ready for all four; ethrex confirmed ready (not yet pushed); Geth agreed to stretch for all four; Besu acknowledged they cannot meet the timeline but did not object to launching with 3 clients.
- Barnabas: "we shouldn't wait for the slowest client... they can always be onboarded later."
- soispoke requested MATCHA and removal of the 1-txn-per-sender limit from EIP-8141 to test multiple concurrent transactions using [EIP-8250](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-8250); noted as desirable but not formally scoped.

sections.heading: Devcon Week ACD Cancellation
sections.summary: ACDE in two weeks (during Devcon) is canceled; next ACDE will be in four weeks.
sections.body:
- The ACDE call in two weeks falls during Devcon.
- No objections to canceling it; ACDE will return in four weeks.
- Ansgar said everything else on the agenda would be postponed to the first ACD after Devcon; no specific items were enumerated on the call.
